name: KernelCI

foundation.via: Run as the KernelCI Foundation, a member-funded Linux Foundation project

summary: Continuous integration for the upstream Linux kernel: it builds kernel trees in many configurations, boots and tests them on real boards in community labs, and collects results from other kernel CI systems in one public database.
intro: The Linux kernel runs on more hardware than any other operating system, and no single company owns all of it. KernelCI is the shared answer. Its pipeline, Maestro, watches dozens of kernel trees; when a branch moves, it builds the kernel in many configurations and architectures and sends boot and test jobs to hardware labs. KernelCI runs no labs itself: member companies and individuals connect theirs, either as LAVA labs that receive jobs pushed from Maestro or as pull-mode labs that poll Maestro’s API from behind a firewall. A single mainline checkout can produce sixty-odd builds, nearly two hundred boots and tens of thousands of test results across well over a hundred hardware platforms.

Results go into KCIDB, a common database with a fixed JSON schema that other kernel CI systems also submit to, such as Red Hat’s CKI, Linaro’s LKFT and syzbot, so one dashboard shows one tree’s results from all of them. The web dashboard at dashboard.kernelci.org, backed by PostgreSQL, lets maintainers browse builds, boots, tests and known issues and subscribe to email reports. `kci-dev` is the command-line client: it lists results, compares two commits to find regressions, can act as a gate in another CI pipeline and, since 2026, serves the same data to AI assistants as an MCP server.

The project is run by the KernelCI Foundation under the Linux Foundation. Its premier members are Arm, the Civil Infrastructure Platform, Collabora, Google, Linaro, Microsoft, Qualcomm, Red Hat and Texas Instruments, and a seven-person technical steering committee, chaired by Ben Copeland of Linaro and including Greg Kroah-Hartman, sets direction. In 2026 regzbot, the kernel’s regression tracker, joined the project, and Linaro donated its TuxMake and TuxRun build and test tools.
strengths: Tests on real hardware that no one company has: boards from many vendors and labs, on architectures from Arm and x86 to RISC-V
One public place for kernel test results, merging KernelCI’s own runs with other CI systems through KCIDB’s shared schema
Labs of any technology can join: LAVA labs receive jobs, and pull-mode labs need only outbound connections to Maestro and KCIDB
Free results for anyone: reading the dashboard or running `kci-dev results` needs no account or token
limits: Built for the upstream Linux kernel and its trees, not as a general CI service for other software
Coverage depends on donated labs: a board is tested only if someone has connected it
It tests branches after they land in a tree; testing patches straight from the mailing list through Patchwork is not available yet
Submitting results or jobs needs a token, requested through a GitHub issue, and private or pre-release work needs a self-hosted instance

story: In 2014 kernel testing was mostly done in private, each company on its own hardware. Arm SoC maintainers Kevin Hilman and Olof Johansson had small board farms at home and began automating boot tests of every tree and emailing the results; with Linaro engineers Tyler Baker and Milo Casagrande, and Alan Bennett, that side project became kernelci.org. By 2016 board farms at Collabora, BayLibre, Linaro, Pengutronix, Free Electrons, TI and others contributed boots, most of them scheduled with Linaro’s LAVA, and by 2017, run by Linaro and BayLibre, it built over 260 configurations per commit and booted them on over 100 boards.

On 28 October 2019, at Open Source Summit Europe in Lyon, KernelCI became a Linux Foundation project with BayLibre, the Civil Infrastructure Platform, Collabora, Foundries.io, Google, Microsoft and Red Hat as founding members. Its goals were better testing of long-term-support kernels, combining the separate kernel testing efforts, and more compute and hardware; KCIDB, a common results database shared with Red Hat’s CKI and Linaro’s LKFT, followed.

The project then rebuilt its own system. The new Maestro pipeline and web dashboard replaced the original service, which was shut down in early 2025, and a Rust KCIDB-ng API replaced the old submission service later that year. Linaro and ELISA joined in 2025, Arm and Qualcomm became premier members in November 2025, and in 2026 regzbot and Linaro’s Tux tools moved under KernelCI.

choices.choice: Labs owned by others, not by the project
choices.why: No single organisation can own every board Linux runs on, so KernelCI schedules work onto labs run by members and individuals and lets each keep its own hardware.

choices.choice: One results schema for every kernel CI
choices.why: Kernel testing was split across separate systems with separate reports. A shared KCIDB schema lets each keep its own pipeline but publish to one database and dashboard.
Corporate labs often cannot expose an API to the internet, so labs can instead poll Maestro and send results to KCIDB, using any lab technology.
Following an “open testing” approach, the dashboard and `kci-dev` need no login to read, so any kernel developer can check a tree before sending a pull request.
